titulo.texto: Community Textile Collection (huipils and traditional looms)

frase_gancho.texto: Fabrics where every thread tells which community you come from.

puente_narrativo.texto: Now we travel across the country by region, and we begin in the Gran Nayar highlands. Look for a wooden panel covered in bright colored yarn, with deer, flowers, and suns.

guion_corto.texto: This is a small sampling of the textiles of Mexico. You will see huipiles, which are long blouses made from rectangular panels of cloth; quechquémitls, which cover the shoulders; wraparound skirts and sashes. Many are woven on the backstrap loom: the weaver ties one end to a tree or a post and the other to her own waist, and tightens the threads with the weight of her body. The materials are white or brown cotton, wool, silk, and ixtle; the colors come from plants and animals, such as indigo, cochineal, and the purple snail. Each community has its own designs, and whoever knows how to read them can tell where the wearer comes from.

guion_largo.texto:
Textiles are the part of history that is almost always lost. The Maya lost theirs to the humidity of the jungle, and from the Candelaria cave we have blankets thanks to the desert. Here, by contrast, you see them alive, woven today and worn by the people who make them. And if you pay attention, you will notice that they keep techniques that were already in use more than a thousand years ago.

The backstrap loom is the main instrument. It is a set of rods: one is tied to a tree or a post, and the other is fastened to a band that the weaver wears around her waist. When she leans back she tightens the threads, and when she moves forward she loosens them. Among the Jaina figurines you saw, there are women weaving with this very same system. More than a thousand years later, the backstrap loom is still in use in many communities.

Notice how a huipil is made. Because the loom produces narrow cloth, two or three rectangular panels are sewn together, an opening is left for the head, and nothing is cut. It is a garment with no waste. Kabal Xook, the woman on the [Yaxchilán lintel](mna_s09_dintel26_yaxchilan), wore a huipil; the basic shape is the same. The quechquémitl, the garment that covers the shoulders, is also a very ancient idea.

The materials tell their own story. Cotton can be white or brown; the brown kind, called coyuchi, grows that way, already colored. Wool arrived with the sheep that the Spaniards brought, and so did silk. Ixtle, the fiber of the maguey, is the same one used to weave the bundles of Candelaria. No material has disappeared: each era added its own.

The colors are a festival of natural chemistry. Indigo gives blue. Cochineal, an insect that lives on the nopal cactus, gives a red so intense that, after the conquest, it was among the most valuable products leaving New Spain for Europe. On the coast of Oaxaca, some weavers dye the thread with a sea snail, the purple snail, and return it alive to the sea. That dye is purple and smells of the sea.

Each community has its own designs, and often whoever knows how to read them can tell which community the wearer comes from. Diamonds, stars, birds, flowers, and serpents repeat with variations. Some of these designs are related to ideas about the world: the diamond, for example, is usually associated with the universe and its four directions. But nothing is fixed: each weaver invents within the tradition.

Among the Maya, the goddess of the moon, medicine, and weaving was Ixchel; among the Mexica, the goddess of weaving was Xochiquétzal. Today many women from different communities continue to weave as an act of memory, and sometimes as their livelihood. A huipil can take months of work, and its price rarely reflects that time.

Explore the other halls with this perspective in mind. The Purépecha rebozo, the [Otomí quechquémitl](mna_s15_quechquemitl_otomi), the [Cuetzalan huipil](mna_s16_huipil_cuetzalan), the Triqui garment, the [Tehuana dress](mna_s17_traje_tehuana), the [Yucatecan terno](mna_s19_terno_yucateco): in each one you will see the same custom of turning a thread into a way of saying who you are.

texto: Find a huipil and count how many panels of cloth it has
Find the backstrap loom and notice the band that the weaver holds around her waist
Compare two garments: which designs repeat in both?

texto.Indigenous People: Amuzgo, Tzotzil, Nahua, Chinantec, Triqui, among others
texto.Region: Oaxaca, Chiapas, Puebla, Guerrero, and Yucatán
texto.Technique/Material: Cotton, wool, silk, natural dyes; woven on a backstrap loom and brocaded
texto.Function: Ceremonial and everyday clothing with high identity value

texto.pregunta: Myth: The embroidery and brocade on huipiles are just decoration.
texto.respuesta: Reality: In many communities the designs identify which community the wearer belongs to, and some preserve ideas about the world. Each weaver learns hers from her family.
